context: premium finishing & material lead-times · finishing-to-MEP interface

brief.intro: New to this project type? A villa is a detached, high-spec house where the schedule is dominated not by structure or building systems but by the finishing trades and the materials behind them. The shell — foundations, blockwork or frame, roof — goes up quickly and is rarely the risk; what drives the programme is the chain from wet-area waterproofing through stone or marble tiling, painting and bespoke joinery, each of which depends on a material or a craftsman that can be slow to secure. Pools and landscaping are common on this type, and their waterproofing and plant work run alongside, and sometimes gate, the main house finishes. Because everything is bespoke and visible, quality control and snagging take longer than on a standard house, and the last mile — joinery fit, fixtures and detailed snagging — is where villa programmes most often slip.

must_get_right: Order long-lead bespoke items — stone, joinery, specialist fixtures — against the finishing programme, not against the move-in date; these are usually the true critical path, not the structure.
Protect the wet-area and pool waterproofing test before tiling starts — a failed test discovered late can undo weeks of finished work built around it.
Sequence the finishing-to-MEP interface deliberately — lighting scenes, smart-home wiring and fixture positions must be resolved before ceilings and walls close, not after.
Budget real time for detailed snagging — bespoke, highly visible finishes generate more defects and more rework cycles than a standard house.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Given its schedule weight, the finishing sequence is modelled activity-by-activity rather than as a single summary bar.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard 6-day working week; waterproofing curing and test durations are held as real non-working time. Specialist stone-fixing and joinery crews sometimes move to an extended single shift near handover to protect the finish date.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs structure & envelope → wet-area/pool waterproofing & test → stone/tiling → bespoke joinery → detailed snagging → handover. Lighting-scene and smart-home wiring for MEP first fix must close out before ceilings and walls finish, or rework follows.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Interior design and material selections frozen before finishing procurement; sample/mock-up approvals obtained before bulk material order; a single client decision-maker for variations.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: Bespoke, imported and specialist items dominate the villa's long-lead list and typically set the true critical path:

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Specialist stone-fixing and joinery crews are scarce and shared across projects; site access for large stone/joinery deliveries needs planning; pool works run alongside main house finishing and compete for the same access route.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: late material or sample approval, a wet-area or pool waterproofing test failure discovered after finishes are in place, and joinery rework from tolerance mismatches. Contingency is held before stone/tiling start and before detailed snagging.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4 for finishing-trade sequencing on site — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
